title: Sextans B
caption: The dwarf galaxy Sextans B, imaged by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: KPNO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. Data obtained and processed by: P. Massey (Lowell Obs.), G. Jacoby, K. Olsen, & C. Smith (AURA/NSF) Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Red patches of star formation glow near the centre of Sextans B, an irregular dwarf galaxy in the constellation Sextans. Around it, several bright stars show crisscross spikes, and many small, fuzzy background galaxies are scattered across the field.

Irregular dwarf galaxies are smaller than the Milky Way and have no tidy spiral or elliptical shape. Sextans B lies around 4.5 million light-years from Earth, in the southern sky, and its red regions mark places where new stars are being born.

The bright, spiky stars are not part of Sextans B at all. They belong to our own galaxy and sit much closer to us, and their crisscross spikes are produced as their light interacts with the structure of the telescope. The fuzzy smudges, by contrast, are galaxies that look tiny because they lie much farther away than Sextans B. The image was captured with the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope.
scale: Sextans B lies around 4.5 million light-years from Earth, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: Taken with the Mosaic I camera on the NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope through broadband U, B, V, R and I filters plus narrow hydrogen-alpha, oxygen and sulfur filters; the colour mapping isn't published.
